article_title: AI Coaching for Accelerating Human Skill Development with Reinforcement Learning
citation: Wei Wang, Enlin Gu, Antonio Loquercio, Haimin Hu, Rahul Mangharam. (2026). AI Coaching for Accelerating Human Skill Development with Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25337
title: Learning to Coach (L2C): an RL pipeline combining adaptive blending, a skill-change PFA, and a surrogate reward
description: L2C is the article's trainable coaching framework built on the Coaching Game formalism. Its contributions are "threefold: (i) a closed-loop blending rule that adapts the assistance levelλto the coach's observations of both the physical environment and the learner behavior; (ii) a reformu-lation of theCoaching Gameto a single-agent POMDP, solvable via RL, through a probabilistic model of the coach's causal influence on learner skill; and (iii) a tractable surrogate reward that is provably consistent with the counterfactual V oI objective." A hybrid probabilistic finite-state automaton models skill change on success and failure events with sigmoid rates over skill; the coach policy is trained with PPO against skill improvement and deployed with Bayesian runtime skill inference and multimodal feedback.
requirements: A pretrained expert policy to anchor the blending rule
A learner model expressible as a skill-parameterized policy class
Privileged access to learner skill during simulation training
constraints: The Boltzmann learner model is one tractable choice; the article states accurately modeling skill-conditioned learner behaviors remains an open problem
Verbal and visual cues are predefined and triggered by fixed rules; only assistance modulation of physical control is learned
target_learners: human learners practicing motor skills such as FPV drone racing, mostly novices
target_learning_goals: accelerated development of independent motor-skill competence, measured by unassisted lap time and failure count
examples: Deployed in a 40-minute FPV drone racing coaching session with shared control, verbal instructions, visual cues, and guided re-attempts of failed segments
key_sources: Wei Wang, Enlin Gu, Antonio Loquercio, Haimin Hu, Rahul Mangharam. (2026). AI Coaching for Accelerating Human Skill Development with Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25337

citation: Yasser Teimouri, Julia Goetze, and Luke Plonsky. (2019). SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYSIS. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 41, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263118000311
title: L2 anxiety as a negatively acting affective variable in L2 learning with (non)linguistic moderators
description: The article frames L2 anxiety as an affective variable with a demonstrably negative role in L2 learning, moderated by linguistic and nonlinguistic variables. It states the study "provides firm evidence for both the negative role of L2 anxiety in L2 learning and the moderating effects of a number of (non)linguistic variables." The framework builds on decades of empirical and theoretical attention to L2 anxiety and its relationship with achievement.
requirements: Measurement of both anxiety (various types) and language achievement to estimate the relationship
constraints: Effect sizes vary across achievement measure types, educational levels, target languages, and anxiety types, so the negative association is not uniform
examples: Meta-analysis of 216 correlations yielding a mean r = −.36
key_sources: Yasser Teimouri, Julia Goetze, and Luke Plonsky. (2019). SECOND LANGUAGE ANXIETY AND ACHIEVEMENT: A META-ANALYSIS. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, Volume 41, Issue 2. https://doi.org/10.1017/S0272263118000311

article_title: Unraveling the nexus among achievement goals, self-efficacy, and motivation regulation and their joint effects on L2 student writers’ writing achievement: a person-based approach
citation: Jianhua Zhang, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Unraveling the nexus among achievement goals, self-efficacy, and motivation regulation and their joint effects on L2 student writers' writing achievement: a person-based approach. Metacognition and Learning (2025) 20:29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09434-0
title: A four-profile taxonomy of L2 writing achievement goals grounded in the trichotomous achievement goal model and person-based (latent profile) analysis
description: The article organizes L2 student writers' motivation via the trichotomous achievement goal model (mastery, performance-approach, performance-avoidance) combined with a person-based latent profile approach. Latent profile analysis yielded four profiles labeled, in the article's words, "Low All Goals (LAGs)", "Mastery High (MH)", "Average All Goals (AAGs)", and "High All Goals (HAGs)". The taxonomy is used to test whether self-efficacy, motivation regulation, and writing achievement differ across learner types rather than across variables. Three profiles matched prevalent profiles in Wormington and Linnenbrink-Garcia's (2017) synthesis, which the authors take as supporting cross-contextual stability of goal adoption patterns.
requirements: Requires measures of mastery, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance writing goals (here the adapted Writing Achievement Goals Scale) and latent profile analysis with fit indices (AIC, BIC, aBIC, entropy, LMR-LRT, BLRT).
constraints: Profiles were identified in a convenience sample of tertiary EFL students in Southwest China; the authors note contextual factors in L2 writing may influence how achievement goals are endorsed.
target_learning_goals: L2 writing achievement and motivation regulation in writing
examples: The study assigned 416 students to the four profiles and compared them on self-efficacy, motivation regulation strategies, and writing achievement in two genres.
key_sources: Jianhua Zhang, Lawrence Jun Zhang. (2025). Unraveling the nexus among achievement goals, self-efficacy, and motivation regulation and their joint effects on L2 student writers' writing achievement: a person-based approach. Metacognition and Learning (2025) 20:29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09434-0

article_title: Ceci n'est pas une explication: Evaluating Explanation Failures as Explainability Pitfalls in Language Learning Systems
citation: Ben Knight, Wm. Matthew Kennedy, Danielle Carvalho, Isaac Pattis, and James Edgell. (2026). Ceci n'est pas une explication: Evaluating Explanation Failures as Explainability Pitfalls in Language Learning Systems. MIRAGE Workshop @ IUI 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26145
title: L2-Bench operationalises the giving-feedback competency through six critical dimensions of effective feedback
description: L2-Bench is an evaluation benchmark for AI systems in language education. For the giving-feedback competency, the authors operationalise the competency of "giving feedback" through a structured evaluation framework examining six critical dimensions: diagnostic accuracy, awareness of appropriacy, causes of error, prioritisation, guidance for improvement, and supporting self-regulation. Each dimension extends beyond simple error correction to encompass considerations essential to effective language teaching feedback.
requirements: Evaluation of AI feedback must assess diagnostic accuracy, appropriacy, causes of error, prioritisation, guidance for improvement, and self-regulation support, not just error correction
constraints: The paper presents only a portion of L2-Bench, focused on the giving-feedback competency
target_learners: language learners using AI-powered learning tools
target_learning_goals: effective feedback in second-language learning, including appropriacy, error diagnosis, and self-regulated learning
examples: The framework structures the paper's analysis of how AI systems may fail in each feedback dimension
key_sources: Ben Knight, Wm. Matthew Kennedy, Danielle Carvalho, Isaac Pattis, and James Edgell. (2026). Ceci n'est pas une explication: Evaluating Explanation Failures as Explainability Pitfalls in Language Learning Systems. MIRAGE Workshop @ IUI 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26145

article_title: Ceci n'est pas une explication: Evaluating Explanation Failures as Explainability Pitfalls in Language Learning Systems
citation: Ben Knight, Wm. Matthew Kennedy, Danielle Carvalho, Isaac Pattis, and James Edgell. (2026). Ceci n'est pas une explication: Evaluating Explanation Failures as Explainability Pitfalls in Language Learning Systems. MIRAGE Workshop @ IUI 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26145
title: L2-Bench: an evaluation benchmark for AI systems in language education
description: L2-Bench is an evaluation benchmark designed to assess the efficacy of AI systems in language learning design. It decomposes the tasks that underpin a learning experience designer into a hierarchical taxonomy of competencies. This paper formalises the portion concerning giving feedback, and the authors document initial efforts to build the benchmark around the explainability-pitfalls concept.
requirements: Evaluation should extend beyond computing an accuracy metric, since feedback failures require a different approach
constraints: A major limitation of the current benchmark is that it does not yet account for multi-turn interaction
target_learners: language learners using AI-powered learning tools
target_learning_goals: evaluation of AI feedback quality in language education
examples: The authors report preliminary evaluation of frontier AI models on L2-Bench tasks for the giving-feedback competency
key_sources: Ben Knight, Wm. Matthew Kennedy, Danielle Carvalho, Isaac Pattis, and James Edgell. (2026). Ceci n'est pas une explication: Evaluating Explanation Failures as Explainability Pitfalls in Language Learning Systems. MIRAGE Workshop @ IUI 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.26145

article_title: L2-Bench: An Evaluation Benchmark for Measuring LLM Capabilities in Second Language Education
citation: James Edgell, Wm. Matthew Kennedy, Ben Knight, Danielle Carvalho, Martin Ku, Isaac Pattis. (2026). L2-Bench: An Evaluation Benchmark for Measuring LLM Capabilities in Second Language Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08842
title: L2-Bench: an open-source benchmark of 1,000+ task-response pairs for L2 learning experience design
description: L2-Bench is an open-source evaluation dataset of 1,000 single-turn task-response pairs operationalizing a taxonomy of second language learning experience design for UK/US L2 English. Tasks are parameterized by "a structured ontology of 33 variables across five dimensions" covering learner characteristics, learning purpose, context, teacher factors, and resources. Items were produced via a hybrid human-AI authoring pipeline with expert review, and each task carries reference answers and a three-layer rubric (consensus, task, and universal criteria) with point values in [-10,+10].
requirements: Tasks must be relevant to authentic professional practice, representative of multiple stakeholder perspectives, clear, and original relative to pretraining data
constraints: Currently scoped to UK/US L2 English as target language
Single-turn interactions only; multi-turn dataset production is future work
target_learners: second language learners of English across primary, secondary, tertiary and adult settings
target_learning_goals: second language learning experience design tasks such as lesson planning, feedback, assessment, and conversational exchange
key_sources: James Edgell, Wm. Matthew Kennedy, Ben Knight, Danielle Carvalho, Martin Ku, Isaac Pattis. (2026). L2-Bench: An Evaluation Benchmark for Measuring LLM Capabilities in Second Language Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08842

article_title: L2-Bench: An Evaluation Benchmark for Measuring LLM Capabilities in Second Language Education
citation: James Edgell, Wm. Matthew Kennedy, Ben Knight, Danielle Carvalho, Martin Ku, Isaac Pattis. (2026). L2-Bench: An Evaluation Benchmark for Measuring LLM Capabilities in Second Language Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08842
title: Taxonomy of 12 competencies and 31 subcompetencies composing second language learning design
description: The article defines the L2 learning design construct as "a novel taxonomy comprising 31 subcompetencies grouped into 12 main competencies". Competencies were identified via a structured review of five influential second language education frameworks (CEFR, Eaquals, Cambridge English Teaching Framework, the Competency Framework for Language Learning Materials Writing, and the British Council CPD Framework) and refined through expert iteration. The taxonomy functions as a sociotechnical boundary object that operationalizes discipline-specific practices for AI system design, and structures the benchmark's dataset and rubrics.
requirements: Expert practitioner validation of task authenticity and criteria adequacy
constraints: Built on frameworks of European origin, which may embed cultural and pedagogical assumptions that do not necessarily transfer to other target languages or non-European traditions
target_learning_goals: the full range of second language learning design competencies, from lesson planning to assessment and conversational exchange
key_sources: James Edgell, Wm. Matthew Kennedy, Ben Knight, Danielle Carvalho, Martin Ku, Isaac Pattis. (2026). L2-Bench: An Evaluation Benchmark for Measuring LLM Capabilities in Second Language Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08842
